evaluated.name: Weakest-Link Cheap And Solvent
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(re, che), lt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A stock is a compensated value opportunity only if it clears both hurdles simultaneously; the payoff is governed by the binding constraint, so the relevant score is the minimum of within-industry cheapness rank and within-industry solvency-buffer rank (retained earnings plus cash minus total liabilities, scaled by assets).
evaluated.reasoning:
MIN is a conjunctive, non-additive interaction that replaces the arbitrary 50/25/25 weighting of the earlier nested SUMRANK — no fixed weights are imposed and a high score is unattainable by excelling on one theme alone. The short leg is economically coherent rather than a mixture of good states: a low minimum means the firm is either richly priced or has an eroded solvency buffer, both of which carry low expected returns, whereas the earlier rank-product's low end contained attractive cheap-unlevered firms.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Distress Sorted Within Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value-trap effect is a within-value phenomenon: conditional on being in the cheapest 30% of the cross-section, higher leverage and weaker cash-flow coverage of liabilities identify firms whose discount reflects impaired solvency, and those firms underperform the healthy cheap firms.
evaluated.reasoning:
Restricting the distress score to the cheap bucket and centering it removes the dominant monotone B/M loading that made the earlier rank product simply re-express the value premium — value stocks now populate both tails of the signal, so the spread is purely the distress gradient inside cheapness. Both legs are economically explicit: the short leg is cheap and highly levered with weak operating cash flow relative to liabilities, the long leg is cheap with low liabilities and strong cash coverage, and non-value firms sit at zero in the middle rather than contaminating either extreme. This is a conditional distress sort, not the unconditional distress anomaly, because the same distress score is switched off outside the value region.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accumulated Deficit Flipped Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(re))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness is a compensated discount for firms with a positive stock of lifetime retained earnings, but for firms carrying an accumulated deficit the same discount reflects capital that has been destroyed and is not coming back, so the value slope flips sign across the retained-earnings state.
evaluated.reasoning: Retained earnings is the single cleanest stock measure of whether a firm has ever generated distributable value, and unlike a leverage ratio it is not mechanically tied to industry capital structure. The bounded rank on the valuation leg keeps negative-book and outlier B/M firms from dominating the Fama-MacBeth slope, while the sign gate produces a fully populated two-sided spread: long cheap firms with real accumulated profits, short equally cheap firms with deficits.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Balance Sheet Repair Weighted Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value premium is earned when the discount is closing because obligations are shrinking; the identical discount alongside a rising liability burden signals a firm financing losses with creditors and should predict poor returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Levels of leverage are slow-moving and largely priced, whereas the annual change in total liabilities over assets is a timely state variable for whether distress is resolving or intensifying, which makes this a direction-of-travel mechanism rather than another static safety screen. The critic's objection to the earlier version is addressed by ranking the valuation leg and by standardizing a winsorized change so that the noisy tail of leverage changes cannot dominate portfolio formation, while centering the multiplier keeps the spread two-sided.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Pretax Loss Chronicity Weighted Yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(pi, 0), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high operating-earnings yield is a compensated discount when the firm has been consistently profitable before tax, and is a distressed-option price when the same yield sits on a five-year record dominated by pretax losses; the value slope should scale with the net count of profitable years.
evaluated.reasoning:
Replacing the tax line with pretax income removes the deferred-tax, valuation-allowance and carryback artifacts the critic identified, since pi is the pre-tax operating verdict rather than a book accounting accrual. The graded net count from minus five to plus five also cures the thin-short-leg problem: loss years are common enough that both tails are densely populated and the multiplier degrades smoothly instead of hinging on one noisy annual sign.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Leverage Created Cheapness Wedge
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ceq, ADD(ceq, lt)), RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: When the equity's share of the capital stack is far smaller at market prices than at book values, the discount is being generated by creditor claims rather than by mispriced assets, and such firms are the distressed lottery segment that underperforms.
evaluated.reasoning:
The two legs no longer share a denominator, so nothing cancels: the measure is identically zero for firms with no liabilities no matter how cheap or expensive they are, which means it cannot collapse into either a pure book-leverage sort or a pure B/M sort. It rises only in the specific corner where cheapness and creditor claims reinforce each other, giving a directly testable value-trap hypothesis with a short leg of levered, market-discounted equity and a long leg of firms the market capitalizes above their book share of capital.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout Yield Per Unit Of Leverage
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(lt, at)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash actually distributed to shareholders is a hard-to-fake solvency signal; a given dividend yield means much more when it is delivered from a lightly obligated balance sheet than when it is squeezed out of a heavily levered one, so the yield should be deflated by the liability burden.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the net-current-asset screen entirely and switches to a payout channel that is not mechanically collinear with book-to-market, because dividends are a discretionary cash commitment rather than an accounting stock. The denominator uses total liabilities over assets, which is bounded away from zero for essentially every operating firm since it includes payables, so the ratio is well behaved and the interaction is inseparable: neither a high payout yield alone nor low leverage alone produces a high score.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheapness With Unstable Earnings Power
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(RANK(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The lottery-like trap in cheap stocks is a second-moment phenomenon: cheap firms whose pretax return on assets swings violently have equity that behaves like a claim on a coin flip, while cheap firms with stable earning power are compensated value.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces a static liquidation-value ratio with a mechanism no archive signal has tested, the volatility of fundamentals rather than their level, which is precisely the "distressed lottery" language of the research brief and is not collinear with book-to-market. Ranking the volatility before standardizing bounds the influence of a few extreme fundamental series, and centering it makes the multiplier two-sided so the sort separates stable cheap firms from unstable cheap firms rather than merely re-ordering the value premium.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Near Term Obligation Wall Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(lct, lt), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes a cheap firm fragile is not how much it owes but when it owes it; when current liabilities are a large fraction of total obligations, the discount is an option on a successful refinancing, whereas long-dated obligations give a cheap firm time for the discount to close.
evaluated.reasoning: Maturity structure is a distress channel that is essentially uncorrelated with profitability and investment, so unlike the retained-earnings and loss-chronicity gates this interaction should not have its long leg absorbed by RMW and CMA, which is exactly why those signals produced positive slopes but negative FF5 alphas. The ratio is bounded between zero and one and defined for every operating firm, giving a dense two-sided spread once centered.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own History Cheapness With Earnings Stock
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(re, lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheap end of its own five-year valuation range has suffered a specific dislocation; that dislocation mean-reverts when lifetime retained earnings are large relative to obligations and confirms permanent impairment when they are not.
evaluated.reasoning: Time-series cheapness is a different valuation concept from cross-sectional book-to-market and loads far less on HML, which directly attacks the reason previous healthy-cheapness signals had their alpha swallowed by the factor model. Scaling retained earnings by total liabilities rather than assets frames the solvency buffer against what the firm actually owes, making the interaction a survival-conditioned mean-reversion bet rather than another quality-value blend.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Obligation Servicing Trend Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(GROWTH(RATIO(revt, lt), 1), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a cheap firm is not whether its debt is growing but whether its business is growing faster than its obligations; rising revenue per dollar of liabilities means the obligation burden is being outrun, while falling revenue per dollar of liabilities means the firm is shrinking into its liability stack.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the liability-change axis entirely, so it is neither the archived deleveraging signal nor its sign flip, and it is not the debt-issuance or asset-growth anomaly: a firm that issues debt while revenue grows proportionally scores neutral, which is exactly the distinction those anomalies cannot make. The multiplier is itself cross-theme, pairing an operating scale measure with total obligations, and its direction follows from solvency arithmetic rather than from reverse-engineering a prior alpha sign.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt Capacity Coverage Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Lenders judge solvency by how many years of operating cash generation it would take to retire the obligations, so a book discount is compensated when EBITDA covers a large share of total liabilities and is a distressed option when coverage is thin or negative.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the capital-structure wedge and the retained-earnings gate entirely and substitutes the actual credit-market solvency metric, EBITDA relative to total liabilities, which is a flow-to-obligation concept rather than the stock-to-asset ratios already in the archive and is scaled by what the firm owes rather than by assets, so it is not a repackaged RMW profitability leg. Loss-making firms fall to the bottom of the coverage rank naturally, giving a monotone, densely populated multiplier without any post-hoc sign choices.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Survival Record Weighted Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUB(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(dvc, 0), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(wcap), 0), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A five-year record of paying cash out to shareholders while never running a working-capital deficit is direct evidence that a firm has survived the cycle without creditor pressure, and cheapness attached to that record is compensated, whereas cheapness attached to years of deficits and no distributions prices genuine impairment.
evaluated.reasoning:
Replacing the dividend change with a five-year count of paying years removes the zero-mass problem the critic identified, since the multiplier takes six distinct levels populated across the cross-section rather than collapsing non-payers and non-changers onto the same point. Subtracting the count of working-capital-deficit years builds a genuine survival record from two independent observable commitments, which is a different construct from the published dividend-change effect and needs no arbitrary flow-over-stock normalization.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Binding Solvency Constraint Revenue Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(MIN(RATIO(wcap, lt), RATIO(re, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency fails at its weakest point, so a cheap firm should be judged by the worse of its liquidity buffer and its lifetime earnings buffer, both measured against total obligations; revenue bought cheaply is compensated only when neither buffer is binding.
evaluated.reasoning:
The archived MIN construct took the minimum across themes, which compressed the valuation leg and left the sorted extremes tie-ridden; here MIN operates strictly inside the distress theme to identify the binding constraint, and the valuation leg enters at full resolution, which is a structurally different use of the operator rather than a re-parameterization. Using revenue-to-price for the valuation leg also moves the long side away from the profitable, conservative, high-book-to-market firms whose returns the five-factor model already spans, which is the diagnosed reason earlier healthy-cheapness signals produced positive slopes but no alpha.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Runway Operating Yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(che, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high operating-earnings yield is compensated when the firm holds enough cash to meet a full year of claims without accessing markets, and is an option on refinancing when the cash balance is a small fraction of what comes due.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash relative to current liabilities is a stock-of-liquidity concept distinct from every flow and composition measure tested so far, and it is the variable that determines whether a firm can wait out a downturn rather than transact into it. Pairing it with the EBITDA yield rather than book-to-market keeps the long leg away from the profitable-conservative-value corner that the five-factor model already spans.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Redeployable Collateral Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(act, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What limits the downside of a cheap firm is the redeployability of what it owns: when the asset base is dominated by current assets that can be converted at close to carrying value, distress resolves through orderly liquidation, whereas a book value locked in specific long-lived assets is realizable only at fire-sale prices to constrained industry buyers.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the liability side entirely and moves to asset-side recovery value, so it is neither a mirror of the maturity-composition result nor any of the coverage, leverage or financing channels already in the archive. The Shleifer-Vishny asset-specificity mechanism predicts that the same book discount carries very different expected recovery depending on asset composition, which is a falsifiable claim about which cheap firms have a floor under their valuation rather than a re-reading of a prior residual.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Covered Dividend Yield Trap
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(pi, dvc), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is the most visible form of cheapness and the most treacherous: it is compensated when pretax earnings comfortably exceed the distribution, and it is a pre-announcement of a cut when the firm is paying out more than it earns.
evaluated.reasoning:
The valuation leg is dividend yield rather than book-to-market, and the distress leg is payout coverage measured as earnings retained after distributions, so neither leg duplicates the coverage, composition or financing channels already evaluated. Using pi minus dvc scaled by assets keeps the multiplier well behaved for loss-makers and non-payers, which is where a raw payout-ratio denominator would invert, and it makes the classic yield-trap distinction directly testable.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Solvency Inflection Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(ACCEL(RATIO(pi, lt)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress resolution is a turning point, not a level: a cheap firm whose pretax earnings per dollar of obligations is still deteriorating but at a decelerating rate has passed the inflection, while accelerating deterioration means the discount has further to go.
evaluated.reasoning:
The second difference of obligation-scaled earnings is a curvature concept that no archive signal uses — the prior entries test levels, first changes, trends and volatilities — and inflection points are precisely where investors extrapolate the recent direction and misprice the turn. Because a decelerating decline can coexist with a still-negative level and a still-negative change, this construct is not a transform of any previously evaluated leg.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unrecognized Tax Shield Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(txt, ebitda), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm that generates operating earnings while remitting little tax is sheltering income under carryforwards accumulated during an earlier crisis; those shields are an off-balance-sheet asset that the depressed price reflects as past distress rather than as future after-tax cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning:
Unlike the earlier tax proposal, the claim here is not that the tax line validates earnings but that a low tax burden on positive operating earnings identifies a survivor of prior distress carrying unpriced shields, which is an asset-recognition mechanism rather than an earnings-quality one. Scaling tax expense by EBITDA rather than by pretax income keeps the denominator away from zero for exactly the firms of interest, and winsorizing bounds the loss-making tail.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capital Structure Instability Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(RANK(VOL(RATIO(lt, at), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness closes when a firm has a settled financing arrangement; a firm whose obligation-to-asset ratio swings from year to year is in continuous renegotiation with creditors, and its equity is a residual claim whose terms keep being rewritten.
evaluated.reasoning:
This is a second-moment measure on the balance sheet rather than on earnings, which distinguishes it from the archived earnings-volatility interaction that failed, and it captures financing instability that neither the level of leverage nor any single annual change can express. Ranking the volatility before standardizing keeps a handful of restructuring firms from dominating the multiplier while preserving a dense two-sided spread of stably financed against serially refinanced cheap firms.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidation Coverage Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(act, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm is safe when its current assets alone could retire every liability on the balance sheet, because creditors can then be paid without touching the going concern; when total obligations exceed liquid assets by a wide margin, the equity discount is a claim on whatever survives a forced sale of operating assets.
evaluated.reasoning: The winning collateral signal used act/at, which measures composition but never compares assets to the claims against them, so this asks whether the alpha comes from liquid asset intensity per se or from liquid assets actually covering obligations — a distinction with different implications for whether leverage matters at all. The multiplier is itself cross-theme and is defined for every operating firm, so the test is clean and does not sacrifice coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Duration Mismatch Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUB(RANK(RATIO(act, at)), RANK(RATIO(lct, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility comes from funding long-lived assets with claims that come due first; a cheap firm whose asset duration is shorter than its liability duration can meet obligations from the natural unwind of its own balance sheet, while the mismatched firm must refinance or sell illiquid assets into a weak market.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the diagnostic counterpart to Signal 3: if the archive's alpha is driven by short duration on both sides, the difference of the two ranks will cancel it, whereas if it is driven by the asset-liability maturity gap the difference will sharpen it, and the two proposals cannot both succeed. Framing distress as a matching problem rather than a level problem is a different economic claim from every leverage, coverage and composition leg previously tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Realizable Collateral And Servicing Capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Surviving distress requires either paying claims from operations or realizing value from assets, so a cheap firm is compensated when it has both operating coverage of its obligations and a liquid asset base, and is a trap when it has neither.
evaluated.reasoning: The two legs have complementary and non-overlapping evidence profiles in the archive — EBITDA over liabilities delivered a 2.22 slope with no alpha, collateral liquidity delivered a 4.73-t alpha with no slope — which is the signature of two distinct sources of information rather than two proxies for one construct. Equal ranking is justified because the legs answer different survival questions, cash-flow service versus asset realization, and the test is explicitly whether the joint signal inherits both forms of evidence.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Best Escape Route Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(MAX(RANK(RATIO(act, lt)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm avoids default if it can pay claims from either of two independent sources, liquid assets or operating cash flow, so what determines whether a discount is compensated is the better of the two escape routes, not their average and not any single one.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the capital-structure wedge entirely, so there is no silent re-signing of a contradicted hypothesis, and it is not the archived collateral signal with a substituted valuation leg because the distress side is a disjunctive aggregation the archive has never used — MIN was tested as a conjunction, MAX encodes the economically correct claim that survival requires only one viable route. The result is deliberately not collinear with act/at: a cash-generating firm with illiquid assets and an asset-rich firm with weak cash flow both score high, and only firms failing on both score low.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Supplier Financed Operating Cycle Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), revt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Non-debt current liabilities scaled by sales measure how much of a firm's operating cycle its counterparties are willing to fund; suppliers reprice terms continuously and pull credit first, so deep trade financing is renewed private certification of viability, and it carries no fixed maturity date at which a cheap firm can be forced into default.
evaluated.reasoning:
Removing short-term debt from current liabilities and deflating by revenue rather than by assets separates counterparty financing from both leverage level and maturity mix, which is exactly the conflation the critic identified in the previous version, and it makes the measure a business-model intensity rather than a balance-sheet composition. It is a level, not a change, so it is not the working-capital accrual construct, and it will not be collinear with the archived act/at winner because asset-light service firms can score high while inventory-heavy firms score low.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Worst Year Coverage Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(oancf, lt), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency is decided in bad states, so the relevant question for a cheap firm is what its cash-flow coverage of obligations looked like in its worst year of the last five; a firm whose trough coverage was still adequate can survive another downturn, while a firm whose trough went deeply negative has already shown how it fails.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the accrual-gap construct with a downside-state statistic that is neither a level, a change, a trend, nor a volatility, and it is not a re-scaling of anything already tested: two firms with identical current coverage and identical variability can have very different trough readings depending on the shape of their distributions. Using the historical minimum rather than the mean is the empirical analogue of a stress test, and it directly targets the tail-risk part of the value-trap story rather than the average-state part every prior coverage leg captured.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Illiquid Asset Productivity Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(at, act)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Collateral liquidity tells you what the realizable part of the balance sheet is worth; the remaining question is whether the illiquid part earns its keep, because fixed assets that generate no operating cash are impairment candidates and the book value anchoring a cheap stock is then fictitious.
evaluated.reasoning: Every distress channel tested so far measures either liabilities or liquid resources, while this measures the cash productivity of the non-realizable asset base, which is precisely the part of book value most likely to be written down and therefore the part that determines whether a low price-to-book is genuine. It is not a profitability ratio in the RMW sense because the deflator is the illiquid asset base rather than total assets or equity, so asset-light firms with modest earnings can rank high and capital-heavy underperformers rank low.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Yield Survival Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The survival interaction should hold for any credible measure of cheapness, and operating cash flow per dollar of price is a valuation measure that does not depend on the accounting book value whose reliability is itself in question for distressed firms.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates the valuation leg of the archive's best signal, testing whether the joint slope-and-alpha result is a property of the survival interaction or an artifact of book-to-market's factor structure, which matters because HML absorption is the diagnosed reason earlier healthy-cheapness signals lost their alpha. A cash-flow-based discount also avoids double-counting the balance sheet on both sides of the product, making the interaction cleaner economically.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: One Year Liquidity Surplus Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lct), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Default happens on a calendar: what determines whether a cheap firm survives the next twelve months is whether its assets convertible within the year plus one year of operating earnings exceed the claims that fall due within that same year.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the rank-blend structure entirely and states the survival condition as a horizon-matched net surplus, which removes both the implicit-weighting problem the critic identified and the stock-versus-flow incoherence, since a one-year flow is being compared to one-year obligations. It is not an incremental leg on the existing composite: firms with abundant collateral but a heavy current maturity load now score negatively, a distinction no ranked-average version can express.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating Asset Discount With Servicing Capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(at, act), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Once liquid assets are netted from both the asset base and the claims against it, what remains is the price the market is charging for the operating business; that operating discount is compensated when operating earnings comfortably cover total obligations and is a trap when they do not.
evaluated.reasoning:
The revision changes the valuation leg rather than the deflator of a distress leg, so it is not the denominator swap the critic rejected, and it introduces a cheapness concept the archive has never tested — operating assets per dollar of net enterprise claims — which strips out the cash and receivables that make book-to-market misleading for balance-sheet-heavy distressed firms. Pairing it with the archive's slope-bearing coverage leg keeps the two components economically independent, one a price and one a capacity.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accounting Distance To Default Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(RATIO(SUB(at, lt), at), VOL(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Insolvency risk is the size of the equity buffer measured in units of the volatility that could consume it, so a cheap firm with a thin buffer and violently swinging operating earnings is a lottery claim while the same buffer attached to stable earnings is a durable cushion.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the aggregation-operator experiment with the structurally correct default object: neither the equity cushion nor earnings volatility is informative alone — the archive's standalone volatility interaction failed precisely because it ignored the buffer — and their ratio is the accounting analogue of distance to default, which no prior signal here constructs. It is a genuinely different distress dimension from collateral and coverage because two firms with identical liquidity and identical coverage can sit at very different numbers of volatility units from insolvency.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Five Year Resource Stock Per Claim
evaluated.expression: RATIO(ADD(act, TS_SUM(ebitda, 5)), ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A buyer of the entire capital stack should ask how many dollars of realizable resources — liquid assets on hand plus the operating earnings the business has actually produced over a full cycle — stand behind each dollar of creditor and shareholder claims outstanding.
evaluated.reasoning:
Cumulating EBITDA over five years converts the flow into a stock measured over a full business cycle, so the numerator is now dimensionally consistent with the collateral term and with the claim stock in the denominator, which was the critic's central objection. The construct is not the enterprise multiple: it is dominated by neither term alone, it rewards realized cycle-long earnings rather than a single year, and it prices resources against creditor claims and equity claims jointly rather than against equity value alone.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: Collateral Quantity And Illiquid Productivity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, SUB(at, act)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm's balance sheet has two parts and each must be defensible: the realizable part should be large, and the unrealizable part should generate cash, because fixed assets that earn nothing are impairment candidates that make the book anchor fictitious.
evaluated.reasoning: This pairs the archive's largest-alpha leg with its highest-Sharpe leg, and unlike the existing best composite the two legs partition the same balance sheet rather than mixing an asset ratio with a claims ratio, so the equal weighting is economically justified as a partition rather than an arbitrary blend. The pair is untested and the components have complementary evidence profiles: collateral supplies alpha with no slope, illiquid productivity supplies slope and Sharpe with little alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Broad Coverage Cash Yield Survival
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(oancf, ib), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The survival interaction should hold on any measure of internally generated cash per dollar of price, and where the cash flow statement is unavailable, income before extraordinary items is the best available measure of that same quantity.
evaluated.reasoning: The cash-flow-yield version of the survival interaction produced the archive's best alpha and Sharpe but on only 7.9% coverage, which is exactly the diagnostic the objective warns about, so this repairs a coverage failure rather than proposing new economics. The substitution is economically justified rather than a blanket patch: for firm-years without a reported operating cash flow, accounting earnings is the same construct measured with more accrual noise, and if the result survives on double the sample the mechanism is not a small-sample artifact.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Blended Discount Survival Interaction
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness measured on a single accounting anchor is noisy precisely for distressed firms, whose book values are stale and whose earnings are volatile, so averaging a balance-sheet discount with an operating-earnings discount identifies the truly cheap firm more reliably before the survival condition is applied.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive entry uses one valuation anchor, so this isolates the measurement quality of the valuation leg while holding the winning survival leg fixed, and reducing measurement error on the leg that scales the interaction should sharpen the cross-sectional slope without changing the economics. It also tests whether the joint result is book-to-market specific, complementing the cash-flow-yield variant from the other direction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Collateral Velocity Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(revt, act))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Current assets are only good collateral if they are moving: receivables that are collected and inventory that sells convert to cash near carrying value, while a slow-turning current asset base is stale inventory and doubtful receivables that will be written down long before a creditor is repaid.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive establishes that the quantity of liquid assets carries large alpha but says nothing about their quality, and turnover is the natural quality metric because it is realized evidence that the assets convert at book value. It is a level rather than a change, so it is not the working-capital accrual construct, and it will separate asset-heavy distributors with fast-moving stock from firms whose balance sheets have quietly filled with unsellable goods.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Purity Of Collateral Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(che, act))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all current assets are equal in a distress state: cash suffers no haircut, while receivables and inventory are discounted heavily by lenders and buyers, so the share of the liquid base that is actually cash determines how much of the stated collateral survives contact with a forced sale.
evaluated.reasoning: This decomposes the archive's dominant alpha channel into its highest-quality component and asks whether the effect comes from cash sitting inside current assets or from the receivable and inventory portion, a question the existing act/at and che/lct results cannot separate because they use different denominators. Together with the velocity signal it forms a two-sided dissection of collateral quality, and the two cannot both be the answer, which makes the batch informative regardless of outcome.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Market Implied Versus Balance Sheet Distress Gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The same firm carries two independent distress readings — the market's, in how small equity value is relative to the claims stacked ahead of it, and the balance sheet's, in how large those claims are relative to assets that can actually be realized — and when the market's reading is far more pessimistic than the balance sheet warrants, the discount is a mispricing rather than a solvency verdict.
evaluated.reasoning:
This is not a horizon or deflator interpolation of any archived surplus construct; it is a disagreement measure that only has content because one leg is priced by the market and the other is measured in accounting resources, so cheapness enters as the source of the gap rather than as a multiplicative scaler. The two ranks use different denominators, market capitalization versus current assets, so nothing cancels, and both tails are economically explicit: the top is heavily market-discounted equity whose liabilities are already covered by liquid assets, the bottom is equity the market treats as safe despite obligations far exceeding realizable resources.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Cushion And Servicing Capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm survives on cash it already holds against claims that fall due, and on operating earnings that cover the whole obligation stack; the haircut-free asset is cash, so the collateral leg of the survival condition should be stated in cash rather than in total current assets.
evaluated.reasoning: The generation-6 decomposition showed that the collateral alpha lives in the cash component and reverses in the receivable and inventory component, so replacing act/at with che/lct inside the archive's best composite should raise the alpha while the coverage leg supplies the cross-sectional slope that cash alone lacks. The two legs use different denominators, near-term claims versus total obligations, so they are not mechanically correlated and the pair is untested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Excess Market Distress With Servicing Capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The right measure of cheapness for this problem is not the book discount but the gap between how distressed the market prices a firm and how distressed its balance sheet says it is; that excess market pessimism is compensated when operating earnings actually cover the obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: The distress gap delivered the archive's best Sharpe and a 3.35 slope as a standalone construct but only a 2.0-t alpha, which is the profile of a valuation measure awaiting a survival condition, exactly as book-to-market behaved before it was interacted. Promoting it from standalone signal to scaling leg is a structural change rather than a variant, and it replaces an accounting anchor with a market-versus-fundamentals disagreement anchor that no interacted signal in the archive has used.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Horizon Matched Liquidity Against Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ADD(che, COALESCE(oancf, ib)), lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The resources available to meet claims due within a year are cash already in hand plus the cash the business generates during that year, and comparing that total to current liabilities is the exact solvency test a lender applies before renewing a facility.
evaluated.reasoning: This unites the archive's strongest alpha leg, the cash stock, with a flow term that carries cross-sectional slope, in a single horizon-matched ratio rather than a rank blend, so it tests whether the stock and flow should be added inside one coverage measure instead of averaged as separate ranks. The COALESCE convention keeps coverage at the full sample by substituting accounting earnings only where the cash flow statement is absent, which the generation-6 test showed preserves the mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Survival Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the survival interaction is a firm-level solvency effect it should hold when each firm is compared with its own industry, whereas if it is a sector tilt toward distributors and asset-light businesses it will disappear once industry means are removed.
evaluated.reasoning: Balance-sheet composition ratios are heavily industry-determined, and the critic has repeatedly flagged that the collateral results may reflect sector membership rather than realizability, so this is the direct falsification test of the archive's central mechanism. It is a deliberate one-operator design isolate whose informational value is diagnostic: a preserved alpha establishes the firm-level reading, a collapsed alpha reveals that four generations of results are an industry bet.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Durable Cash Cushion Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(che, lct), 0), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cash balance that has covered near-term claims in year after year is a structural feature of the business model, whereas cash held for a single year is usually the proceeds of an emergency raise or an asset sale by a firm already in trouble; only the durable cushion should mark a cheap firm as safe.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the velocity diagnostic, whose sign the archive had already contradicted, and instead asks a question the cash-purity result cannot answer: whether the large cash alpha reflects a persistent characteristic or a transient balance that will be consumed. The five-year count is a graded zero-to-five multiplier with both tails populated, and it separates chronically liquid firms from firms whose cash arrived with dilution or divestment, which is precisely the healthy-versus-distressed distinction the brief asks for.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Net Resource Surplus Against All Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, ebitda), lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency is an accounting inequality, not an average of scores: cash on hand plus a year of operating earnings must exceed the obligations outstanding, and a cheap firm on the wrong side of that inequality is a distressed option regardless of how strong either component looks in isolation.
evaluated.reasoning:
This is not an average of previously tested anchors — it changes the functional form from a rank blend, in which a strong coverage leg can fully offset an empty cash balance, to a net surplus in which the two resources are added and the claims subtracted, so firms fail whenever the identity fails. The components are the ones the archive's decompositions selected, cash rather than total current assets as the collateral term and total liabilities rather than current liabilities as the claim term, and the tested surplus construct used neither, so the economic statement and the portfolio it forms are both distinct.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Cash Cushion Survival
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash holdings are the most sector-determined item on the balance sheet, so a cash cushion is informative about distress only relative to what is normal for the firm's industry; measured that way it should predict returns rather than merely reproduce a sector tilt.
evaluated.reasoning: The cash-based composite delivered a 5.6% alpha at t = 3.85 but a Sharpe of only 0.16 and no cross-sectional slope, the profile of a factor-hedged sector bet, and the identical neutralization repaired exactly that profile for the collateral composite. This is the diagnostic that decides whether the cash channel is a real firm-level survival characteristic or an industry artifact, and it directly repairs the archive's most conspicuous alpha-without-Sharpe failure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Excess Market Distress With Neutral Liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When the market prices a firm as far more distressed than its balance sheet warrants, that excess pessimism is compensated only if the firm holds an industry-adjusted cushion of cash and earns enough to cover its obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: The distress-gap valuation leg paired with a plain coverage rank gave a 2.39 slope but only a 1.59 alpha t-statistic, and the diagnosis is that its survival leg was both too narrow and sector-contaminated, so this pairs it with the neutralized liquidity-plus-coverage score instead. It also removes the mechanical overlap the critic identified, since act now appears only in the valuation leg and the survival leg is built from cash and earnings.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own History Discount With Neutral Survival
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheap end of its own five-year valuation range has suffered a specific dislocation rather than being structurally cheap, and that dislocation mean-reverts when the firm's industry-adjusted collateral and coverage say it will survive the episode.
evaluated.reasoning: Time-series cheapness and industry neutralization attack the same problem from opposite sides — one removes the permanent cross-sectional component of book-to-market, the other removes the sector component of the survival score — so combining them should isolate the firm-specific dislocation the mechanism is meant to price. The archive's earlier own-history construct was handicapped by a weak solvency partner and still produced a 1.93 slope, and it is now paired with the strongest survival score available.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Deep Value Concentrated Survival
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The trap-versus-opportunity distinction only binds in the deep-value tail: for moderately priced firms solvency is already reflected in the price, while for the most heavily discounted firms the market is pricing a probability of failure, so the survival score should receive convex rather than linear weight in cheapness.
evaluated.reasoning:
This is a functional-form hypothesis about where the interaction lives, not another neutralization knob: squaring the valuation rank concentrates the survival tilt in the cheapest quintile and suppresses it through the middle of the distribution, which is exactly what the value-trap story predicts and what a linear scaler cannot express. Because the weighting change is confined to the valuation leg, a gain over the archive's neutralized composite identifies the deep-value tail as the source of the effect rather than the cross-section as a whole.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Improving Peer Solvency Standing Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))), 1), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Every successful construct in this archive is a static snapshot, yet what resolves a distressed discount is movement: a cheap firm climbing its industry's solvency ranking is repairing itself, while a cheap firm sliding down it is deteriorating even if its current level still looks adequate.
evaluated.reasoning:
This adds the missing dynamic dimension rather than repeating an industry-adjustment test on a third static base, and it differs from the archive's failed leverage-change signal in both content and construction, since it tracks the change in a firm's peer-relative standing on collateral and coverage jointly rather than the raw change in one liability ratio. Measuring the change after industry adjustment also removes sector-wide cyclical swings, so the multiplier isolates firm-specific repair and decline.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Priced Distress Contradicted By Coverage
evaluated.expression: IND_ZSCORE(MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The compensated corner requires both conditions at once — the market must have stacked creditor claims high relative to equity value and operating earnings must still cover those claims — because only that conjunction identifies a firm the market treats as distressed while its cash flow says otherwise.
evaluated.reasoning:
Replacing SUMRANK with MIN makes the expression implement the conjunction the hypothesis actually states: a low-leverage, high-coverage firm can no longer score at the top, so the signal is not a sum of the market-leverage and profitability anomalies but a disagreement measure that requires both readings simultaneously. The bottom of the sort is also economically coherent, containing firms the market prices as safe and firms whose earnings fail to cover obligations, both of which carry low expected returns under the value-trap hypothesis.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Selectively Neutralized Survival Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ADD(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(act, at)), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Asset composition is meaningful only relative to industry norms, since a distributor and a utility have structurally different liquid shares, but the ability to cover obligations from operating earnings is an absolute solvency test that means the same thing in every sector and should not be neutralized.
evaluated.reasoning: Full neutralization raised alpha and Sharpe but cost cross-sectional slope (3.14 down to 2.34), and this diagnoses why: neutralizing the coverage leg discards the absolute solvency information that generated the slope in the first place. Applying the industry adjustment only where sector composition genuinely distorts the measurement is a substantive claim about which distress dimension is relative and which is absolute, and it is the one construct in this batch that could improve both metrics at once.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Trough Survival Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(TS_MIN(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt)), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year's balance sheet can be flattered by an asset sale or a good quarter, so the survival condition that matters for a cheap firm is the weakest reading of its collateral and coverage over the recent past, which is what a creditor's covenant history actually reflects.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's one trough-based test used a single narrow leg (oancf/lt) and failed, but the trough of the full survival composite is a different object: it asks whether the firm's joint resources-to-claims position ever broke down, which distinguishes durably solvent firms from firms whose current strength is one year old. It is the only construct in this batch with a time dimension, so it tests whether the mechanism is about a state or about the persistence of that state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Rigid Claims And Coverage Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ADD(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all claims can force a liquidation: suppliers, employees and tax authorities renegotiate, while bond and bank debt is enforced on schedule, so a cheap firm is safe when its earnings cover its obligations and those obligations are mostly renegotiable rather than contractual.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the collateral leg with claim rigidity, a dimension that appears in no accepted signal and is conceptually distinct from how much a firm owns or earns — it concerns who can pull the trigger — so it is new economic content rather than an operator substitution. The neutralization is applied only to the rigidity ratio, whose level is set by industry financing conventions, while absolute coverage is left cross-sectional, following the selective-neutralization logic that a solvency test means the same thing in every sector.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Solvency Sign Gated Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency is a discrete condition rather than a continuous score: either realizable assets plus a year of operating earnings cover every claim or they do not, and the value premium should be earned on one side of that line and reversed on the other.
evaluated.reasoning:
Nine generations of continuous, centered survival scores have never tested the hard inequality as a gate, and the distinction matters economically because a firm one dollar short of covering its claims is qualitatively different from one comfortably above, whereas a z-score treats the difference as marginal. The gate produces a genuinely different portfolio — long cheap solvent firms, short equally cheap insolvent ones, with expensive firms near zero on both sides — and it needs no deflator, no winsorization and no industry adjustment, so it is the most parsimonious statement of the mechanism the archive has produced.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Prefunded Purchase Price Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters to an equity buyer is how much of the price paid is already funded by resources net of every claim, so the survival surplus should be scaled by market capitalization rather than by assets: a discount is compensated when a large share of the purchase price is pre-funded and is an option premium when the surplus is negative.
evaluated.reasoning:
Every surplus construct in the archive deflates by total assets, an accounting scale with no bearing on what an investor pays, whereas deflating by price makes the distress leg itself a valuation statement and changes the ranking materially for firms whose market value has collapsed relative to their book. This is a re-specification of the measurement basis with a clear economic rationale rather than a second refinement stacked onto a tested construct.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Net Exposure Survival Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(wcap, at), RATIO(ebitda, SUB(lt, che)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross balance-sheet measures double count: current assets are pledged against current liabilities and cash is held against debt, so the survival condition should be stated in net terms — working capital after operating claims, and earnings against obligations net of the cash that can retire them.
evaluated.reasoning:
This is not a proxy substitution for coverage purposes but a re-specification of both legs from gross to net exposure, which changes the ranking for exactly the firms the mechanism cares about: a cash-rich, payables-financed firm looks ordinary on act/at and EBITDA/lt but strong on net working capital and net-debt coverage. Netting also removes the mechanical inflation of both legs for working-capital-intensive businesses, which is the residual industry effect that neutralization alone only partially handles.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Loss-Persistence Gated Value
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), SIGN(MA(ib, 3)))
considered.hypothesis: A high book-to-market ratio signals a discount for firms with persistently positive earnings but signals impaired asset value (lottery-like distress) for firms with persistent losses, so the value effect should reverse sign across the profitability regime.
considered.reasoning: The sign flip converts deeply cheap chronic losers from the long leg into the short leg, which is exactly where value strategies historically bleed. Smoothing income over three years prevents a single transitory write-off from misclassifying a healthy firm. This is a genuine interaction because the valuation slope is multiplied by a distress state rather than merely adjusted for it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Deleveraging Value
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap stocks pay off when the balance sheet is repairing; the same discount alongside rising leverage reflects a firm funding losses with debt and should predict poor returns.
considered.reasoning: The level of leverage is slow-moving and largely priced, whereas the annual change in leverage is a timely state variable for whether distress is resolving or intensifying. Multiplying the valuation discount by the deleveraging rate makes the value premium conditional on credit-risk improvement rather than on static solvency. This gives a different mechanism from level-based screens because it captures the direction of the distress process.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Weakest-Link Cheap And Solvent
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(re, che), lt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A stock is a compensated value opportunity only if it clears both hurdles simultaneously; the payoff is governed by the binding constraint, so the relevant score is the minimum of within-industry cheapness rank and within-industry solvency-buffer rank (retained earnings plus cash minus total liabilities, scaled by assets).
considered.reasoning:
MIN is a conjunctive, non-additive interaction that replaces the arbitrary 50/25/25 weighting of the earlier nested SUMRANK — no fixed weights are imposed and a high score is unattainable by excelling on one theme alone. The short leg is economically coherent rather than a mixture of good states: a low minimum means the firm is either richly priced or has an eroded solvency buffer, both of which carry low expected returns, whereas the earlier rank-product's low end contained attractive cheap-unlevered firms.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Rollover-Gap Weighted Earnings Yield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at), 2))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness is rewarded only when the firm does not face a near-term refinancing wall; the same earnings yield is a trap when maturing short-term debt exceeds cash on hand, because equity holders bear the rollover option's downside.
considered.reasoning:
This abandons the published enterprise-multiple ratio entirely and instead makes the valuation slope a function of a specific, timing-based distress state — cash minus debt in current liabilities — so the signal flips sign across the funding-gap boundary rather than merely re-scaling price by leverage. Using a percentile rank for the earnings-yield leg keeps that leg non-negative, so the sign is set by the rollover gap and the magnitude by cheapness, avoiding the perverse quadrant where a loss-making firm with a maturity wall would score positively. The gap is defined for every firm including debt-free ones (dlc = 0 simply yields cash-to-assets), so no observations are dropped or mis-gated.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-Burn Persistence Weighted Sales Yield
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), SUB(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(oancf, 0), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Revenue bought cheaply is valuable when the business has consistently self-funded, and is a distressed-lottery claim when the same revenue has been produced alongside repeated years of negative operating cash flow; the value slope should therefore scale with the net count of self-funding years over the last five.
considered.reasoning:
This removes the ill-defined coverage denominator that broke on zero-debt firms — the multiplier only needs the sign of operating cash flow, which exists for every reporting firm — and it replaces the lossy 0/1 switch with a graded score running from -5 to +5, so the short leg is cheap chronic cash burners rather than a discarded subsample. Persistence over five years, rather than a one-year snapshot, is the economically correct distress state because a single negative cash-flow year is often investment-driven while five are a solvency verdict. Expensively priced firms receive a small sales yield and therefore sit near the middle regardless of their burn history, so the spread is driven by the interaction rather than by either theme alone.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Distress Sorted Within Value
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
considered.hypothesis: The value-trap effect is a within-value phenomenon: conditional on being in the cheapest 30% of the cross-section, higher leverage and weaker cash-flow coverage of liabilities identify firms whose discount reflects impaired solvency, and those firms underperform the healthy cheap firms.
considered.reasoning:
Restricting the distress score to the cheap bucket and centering it removes the dominant monotone B/M loading that made the earlier rank product simply re-express the value premium — value stocks now populate both tails of the signal, so the spread is purely the distress gradient inside cheapness. Both legs are economically explicit: the short leg is cheap and highly levered with weak operating cash flow relative to liabilities, the long leg is cheap with low liabilities and strong cash coverage, and non-value firms sit at zero in the middle rather than contaminating either extreme. This is a conditional distress sort, not the unconditional distress anomaly, because the same distress score is switched off outside the value region.
REASONING_END

considered.name: Accumulated Deficit Flipped Value

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(che, lct))))

considered.hypothesis: What limits the downside of a cheap firm is the redeployability of what it owns: when the asset base is dominated by current assets that can be converted at close to carrying value, distress resolves through orderly liquidation, whereas a book value locked in specific long-lived assets is realizable only at fire-sale prices to constrained industry buyers.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(pi, dvc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is the most visible form of cheapness and the most treacherous: it is compensated when pretax earnings comfortably exceed the distribution, and it is a pre-announcement of a cut when the firm is paying out more than it earns.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(ACCEL(RATIO(pi, lt)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Distress resolution is a turning point, not a level: a cheap firm whose pretax earnings per dollar of obligations is still deteriorating but at a decelerating rate has passed the inflection, while accelerating deterioration means the discount has further to go.

The second difference of obligation-scaled earnings is a curvature concept that no archive signal uses — the prior entries test levels, first changes, trends and volatilities — and inflection points are precisely where investors extrapolate the recent direction and misprice the turn. considered.name: Unrecognized Tax Shield Cheapness

considered.hypothesis: A cheap firm that generates operating earnings while remitting little tax is sheltering income under carryforwards accumulated during an earlier crisis; those shields are an off-balance-sheet asset that the depressed price reflects as past distress rather than as future after-tax cash flow.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(RANK(VOL(RATIO(lt, at), 5)))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness closes when a firm has a settled financing arrangement; a firm whose obligation-to-asset ratio swings from year to year is in continuous renegotiation with creditors, and its equity is a residual claim whose terms keep being rewritten.

This is a second-moment measure on the balance sheet rather than on earnings, which distinguishes it from the archived earnings-volatility interaction that failed, and it captures financing instability that neither the level of leverage nor any single annual change can express. considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(act, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: A cheap firm is safe when its current assets alone could retire every liability on the balance sheet, because creditors can then be paid without touching the going concern; when total obligations exceed liquid assets by a wide margin, the equity discount is a claim on whatever survives a forced sale of operating assets.
considered.reasoning: The winning collateral signal used act/at, which measures composition but never compares assets to the claims against them, so this asks whether the alpha comes from liquid asset intensity per se or from liquid assets actually covering obligations — a distinction with different implications for whether leverage matters at all. The multiplier is itself cross-theme and is defined for every operating firm, so the test is clean and does not sacrifice coverage.

considered.name: Duration Mismatch Cheapness
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUB(RANK(RATIO(act, at)), RANK(RATIO(lct, lt)))))
considered.hypothesis: Fragility comes from funding long-lived assets with claims that come due first; a cheap firm whose asset duration is shorter than its liability duration can meet obligations from the natural unwind of its own balance sheet, while the mismatched firm must refinance or sell illiquid assets into a weak market.

Framing distress as a matching problem rather than a level problem is a different economic claim from every leverage, coverage and composition leg previously tested.

considered.name: Realizable Collateral And Servicing Capacity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: Surviving distress requires either paying claims from operations or realizing value from assets, so a cheap firm is compensated when it has both operating coverage of its obligations and a liquid asset base, and is a trap when it has neither.

considered.name: Best Escape Route Cheapness
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(MAX(RANK(RATIO(act, lt)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt)))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm avoids default if it can pay claims from either of two independent sources, liquid assets or operating cash flow, so what determines whether a discount is compensated is the better of the two escape routes, not their average and not any single one.

This drops the capital-structure wedge entirely, so there is no silent re-signing of a contradicted hypothesis, and it is not the archived collateral signal with a substituted valuation leg because the distress side is a disjunctive aggregation the archive has never used — MIN was tested as a conjunction, MAX encodes the economically correct claim that survival requires only one viable route. considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), revt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Non-debt current liabilities scaled by sales measure how much of a firm's operating cycle its counterparties are willing to fund; suppliers reprice terms continuously and pull credit first, so deep trade financing is renewed private certification of viability, and it carries no fixed maturity date at which a cheap firm can be forced into default.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(oancf, lt), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Solvency is decided in bad states, so the relevant question for a cheap firm is what its cash-flow coverage of obligations looked like in its worst year of the last five; a firm whose trough coverage was still adequate can survive another downturn, while a firm whose trough went deeply negative has already shown how it fails.

This replaces the accrual-gap construct with a downside-state statistic that is neither a level, a change, a trend, nor a volatility, and it is not a re-scaling of anything already tested: two firms with identical current coverage and identical variability can have very different trough readings depending on the shape of their distributions. considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(at, act)))))

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lct), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Default happens on a calendar: what determines whether a cheap firm survives the next twelve months is whether its assets convertible within the year plus one year of operating earnings exceed the claims that fall due within that same year.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(at, act), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
